court: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York
key_provisions: Applies to civil matters before Judge Ho except civil pro se cases.
Use of generative AI to generate any portion of a filing triggers a separate declaration.
The declaration must disclose AI use and certify source review, accuracy, and Rule 11 compliance.
summary: Judge Dale E. Ho’s January 8, 2026 civil individual practices for represented civil matters require any party using generative AI to generate part of a motion, brief, pleading, or other filing to attach a separate declaration disclosing AI use and certifying review of source material, accuracy, and Rule 11 compliance.
text_excerpt: "Any party who uses generative artificial intelligence ... must attach to the filing a separate declaration disclosing the use of artificial intelligence"
title: Individual Rules and Practices in Civil Cases: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence

court: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York
key_provisions: Applies to all civil cases involving pro se litigants before Judge Ho.
Generative AI use to generate any portion of a filing requires a separate declaration.
The declaration must disclose AI use and certify source review and accuracy.
summary: Judge Dale E. Ho’s January 8, 2026 civil pro se practices require any party in a civil pro se case who uses generative AI to generate part of a motion, brief, pleading, or other filing to attach a separate declaration disclosing AI use and certifying source review and accuracy.
text_excerpt: "Any party who uses generative artificial intelligence ... must attach to the filing a separate declaration disclosing the use of artificial intelligence"
title: Individual Practices in Civil Pro Se Cases: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence

court: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York
key_provisions: Applies to criminal cases before Judge Ho.
Use of generative AI to generate any portion of a filing requires a separate declaration.
The declaration must certify source review, accuracy, and Rule 11 compliance.
summary: Judge Dale E. Ho’s revised January 8, 2026 criminal individual practices require any party using generative AI to generate part of a motion, brief, pleading, or other filing to attach a separate declaration disclosing AI use and certifying source review, accuracy, and Rule 11 compliance.
text_excerpt: "Any party who uses generative artificial intelligence ... must attach to the filing a separate declaration disclosing the use of artificial intelligence"
title: Individual Rules and Practices in Criminal Cases: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence

court: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York
key_provisions: Any party using generative AI in preparation of filed documents must disclose that AI was used.
If generative AI drafts filed documents, the party must certify independent review and verification.
The certification covers citations, quotations, legal authority, and Rule 11 obligations.
The rule excludes AI embedded in legal search engines such as Westlaw and LexisNexis.
sanctions_language: "Failure to comply with this rule may result in sanctions, the document being stricken"
summary: Judge Vernon S. Broderick’s October 29, 2025 civil rules require any party, pro se or represented, using generative AI in preparing documents filed with the court to disclose that use. If AI drafts filed documents, the party must certify independent review and verification of citations, quotations, legal authority, and Rule 11 compliance.
text_excerpt: "must further certify in the document that it has independently reviewed and verified the accuracy"
title: Individual Rules & Practices in Civil Cases: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence

court: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York
key_provisions: Counsel is responsible for accurate representations of the record, history, and legal authorities.
Use of ChatGPT or similar tools is not prohibited.
Counsel must personally confirm the accuracy of research conducted with those tools.
summary: Judge Arun Subramanian’s civil individual practices, revised May 11, 2026, state that use of ChatGPT or similar tools is not prohibited. Counsel remain responsible for complete and accurate representations of the record, procedural history, and legal authorities, and must personally confirm the accuracy of research done with those tools.
text_excerpt: "Use of ChatGPT or other such tools is not prohibited, but counsel must at all times personally confirm"
title: Individual Practices in Civil Cases: Use of ChatGPT and Other Tools

court: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York
key_provisions: Applies to submissions prepared using generative AI such as ChatGPT, Harvey, CoCounsel, or Google Bard.
The submitting party and counsel must confirm accuracy and Rule 11 compliance.
Parties and counsel remain responsible for the accuracy of submissions.
sanctions_language: "Failure to uphold this responsibility may result in sanctions or other corrective or disciplinary action."
summary: Judge Analisa Torres’s revised November 5, 2025 civil individual practices remind parties and counsel of Rule 11 duties and require a submitting party and counsel to confirm for themselves that any submission prepared with generative AI, and all source material within it, is accurate and Rule 11 compliant.
text_excerpt: "must confirm for themselves that the submission, and all source material within, is accurate"
title: Individual Practices in Civil Cases: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence

court: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York
key_provisions: Applies to attorneys using GAI in filings before Judge Clarke.
Also applies to serving or delivering discovery requests, responses, or objections.
The rule points attorneys to Rules 11(b), 26(g), other relevant rules, and ethical rules.
summary: Judge Jessica G. L. Clarke’s January 2026 civil individual practices state that any attorney using generative artificial intelligence in connection with a court filing or with discovery requests, responses, or objections must comply with Rules 11(b), 26(g), other relevant rules, and applicable ethical rules.
text_excerpt: "Any attorney using Generative Artificial Intelligence ... must comply with Rule 11(b) and Rule 26(g)"
title: Individual Rules and Practices in Civil Cases: Artificial Intelligence

court: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York
key_provisions: All litigants are responsible for verifying output produced by an AI tool.
An attorney signing an AI-assisted filing must attach a signed certification.
The certification must address review and verification of cited legal authorities and factual assertions.
sanctions_language: "The Court may impose sanctions on counsel and/or strike the filing"
summary: Judge John P. Cronan’s revised October 23, 2025 civil rules require an attorney signing an AI-assisted filing to attach a signed certification stating whether the litigant personally reviewed the filing for accuracy and, if so, describing steps taken to verify legal authorities and factual assertions generated by AI.
text_excerpt: "must attach to the filing a signed certification ... describing in detail the steps taken to verify"
title: Individual Rules and Practices in Civil Cases: Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools

court: U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York
key_provisions: Litigants remain responsible for legal documents produced with technology assistance.
The rule identifies ChatGPT, Google Bard, Bing AI Chat, and generative AI services as examples.
Litigants must review and verify computer-generated content for compliance with Rule 9011.
summary: The Southern District of New York Bankruptcy Court’s amended September 30, 2024 Local Bankruptcy Rule 9011-1 cautions litigants that technologies including ChatGPT, Google Bard, Bing AI Chat, and generative AI services may produce inaccurate content and requires review and verification of computer-generated content for Rule 9011 compliance.
text_excerpt: "must review and verify any computer-generated content to ensure it complies with all such standards"
title: Local Bankruptcy Rule 9011-1: Signing of Papers

court: Supreme Court of New Jersey
key_provisions: Lawyers must check and verify all AI-generated information to ensure accuracy.
The RPCs do not require lawyers to disclose AI use to the court.
Lawyers remain responsible for pleadings, arguments, evidence, and client communications using AI.
Lawyers must ensure AI system security before entering non-public client information.
summary: The New Jersey Supreme Court’s January 24, 2024 Notice to the Bar provides preliminary AI guidelines for New Jersey lawyers. It states lawyers have an ethical duty to check and verify AI-generated information, remain responsible for pleadings, arguments, and evidence, and that the RPCs do not require court disclosure of AI use.
text_excerpt: "Because AI can generate false information, a lawyer has an ethical duty to check and verify all information generated by AI"
title: Notice to the Bar: Preliminary Guidelines on the Use of Artificial Intelligence by New Jersey Lawyers

court: U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey
key_provisions: All matters pending before Judge Padin, including pro se matters, are covered unless stated otherwise.
Any GAI use in court filings requires mandatory human-review certification.
The review should include correcting errors and eliminating hallucinations.
Noncompliance may lead to sanctions, striking, or bar referral.
sanctions_language: "may result in sanctions, such as the filing being stricken"
summary: Judge Evelyn Padin’s revised May 28, 2026 general pretrial and trial procedures require mandatory certification for any generative AI use in court filings. The certification must state that the GAI work product was diligently reviewed by a human being for accuracy and applicability, including correcting errors and eliminating hallucinations.
text_excerpt: "requires a mandatory certification that the GAI work product was diligently reviewed by a human being"
title: General Pretrial and Trial Procedures: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence

court: U.S. District Court for the District of Connecticut
key_provisions: Attorneys and pro se litigants should use great caution with AI-generated language.
Use of AI without verification implicates Rule 11.
The court has a no-tolerance policy for hallucinated legal propositions or severe misstatements of law.
sanctions_language: "Such filings will often result in sanctions absent reasonable excuse."
summary: The District of Connecticut’s September 12, 2025 notice tells attorneys and pro se litigants to exercise great caution when submitting AI-generated language in filings. It warns that unverified AI output implicates Rule 11 and that briefing, AI-assisted or not, hallucinating legal propositions or misstating law will often result in sanctions.
text_excerpt: "the Court has a no-tolerance policy for any briefing (AI-assisted or not) that hallucinates legal propositions"
title: Notice to Counsel and Litigants Regarding AI-Assisted Research

court: Connecticut Superior Court
key_provisions: Section 4-9 defines generative AI and covers court-filed documents.
A person using generative AI to create or edit a filing must independently verify AI-produced citations, legal authorities, or evidence.
By filing, a person represents good-faith diligent efforts to comply with the rule.
The Section 4-2 signature certification incorporates Section 4-9 compliance.
sanctions_language: "may result in court-imposed sanctions, including, without limitation, the entry of a nonsuit or default judgment."
summary: The Connecticut Superior Court’s June 23, 2026 Practice Book amendments add Section 4-9 on generative AI compliance and revise Section 4-2. Anyone using generative AI to create or edit a court-filed document must independently verify all AI-produced citations, legal authorities, or evidence, and filing represents diligent compliance.
text_excerpt: "shall independently verify all citations, legal authorities or evidence produced by generative AI"
title: Practice Book Amendments: Generative Artificial Intelligence Compliance

court: Delaware Judiciary
key_provisions: The policy applies to authorized users in official duties and on state technology resources.
Authorized users are responsible for GenAI output accuracy and must use caution.
Decision-making functions may not be delegated to approved GenAI.
Non-public information may not be input into non-approved GenAI, and non-approved GenAI may not be used on state resources.
summary: The Delaware Supreme Court’s October 21, 2024 order adopts an interim GenAI policy for judicial officers, employees, law clerks, interns, externs, and volunteers. Authorized users remain responsible for GenAI output, may not delegate decision-making to GenAI, and may not enter non-public information into non-approved GenAI tools.
text_excerpt: "Authorized Users may not delegate their decision-making function to Approved GenAI."
title: Order Adopting Interim Policy on the Use of GenAI by Judicial Officers and Court Personnel

court: Unified Judicial System of Pennsylvania
key_provisions: Personnel may only use or install GenAI tools approved by leadership.
Permitted uses include summaries, preliminary legal research, initial drafts, editing public documents, and public chatbots.
Personnel must understand technical capabilities and limitations and remain responsible for accuracy.
Personnel shall not share non-public information with non-secured AI systems.
summary: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court approved an interim GenAI policy on September 9, 2025, effective December 8, 2025, for judicial officers and Unified Judicial System personnel. Personnel may use approved GenAI for listed work purposes, must understand tool limits, remain responsible for accuracy, and may not share non-public information with non-secured AI systems.
text_excerpt: "humans must review GenAI output and Personnel are responsible for the accuracy"
title: Interim Policy on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence by Judicial Officers and Court Personnel

court: Massachusetts State Courts
key_provisions: The guidelines cover Massachusetts state-court judges, clerks, employees, law clerks, interns, contractors, registers, and recorders.
GenAI may not be used for legal research, legal writing, or other legal work at this time.
Administrative use is allowed only with approved tools, opt-out settings, and Level 1 Public Data.
Users must never rely on GenAI as the sole reference or for final decisions and must independently verify output.
notes: Mass.gov page was read through the fetch tool after direct curl returned a 403 challenge.
summary: The Massachusetts state courts’ interim GenAI guidelines apply to judges, clerks, registers, recorders, employees, law clerks, interns, and contractors. The guidelines state GenAI may not be used for legal research, legal writing, or other legal work, and allow only approved tools for administrative tasks using public data with retention and training safeguards.
text_excerpt: "Can I use GenAI tools to assist with legal research, legal writing, or other legal work? Not at this time."
title: Interim Guidelines for Use of Generative AI

court: New York State Unified Court System
key_provisions: Applies to all judges and nonjudicial UCS employees for UCS-owned devices and UCS-related work.
Only DoTCR-approved generative AI products may be used.
Users need initial and continuing AI training before using generative AI products.
Confidential, private, privileged, PII, protected health, and court-filed documents may not be entered into non-private models.
Users must thoroughly review AI-produced content for accuracy, appropriateness, and unfair bias.
summary: The New York State Unified Court System’s interim AI policy, effective October 2025, governs judges and nonjudicial employees using AI for UCS work. It requires approved products, mandatory training, restrictions on confidential or filed documents in non-private models, and thorough review for accuracy, appropriateness, and unfair bias.
text_excerpt: "No generative AI product may be used on any UCS-owned device or for any UCS-related work until the user has completed the initial training course."
title: New York State Unified Court System Interim Policy on the Use of Artificial Intelligence

court: New York State Unified Court System
key_provisions: Part 161 applies to all UCS courts in civil and criminal cases.
AI use by attorneys and parties in preparing court papers should not be prohibited if existing duties are met.
Attorneys and parties should not be required to disclose AI use upon submitting papers.
Courts may adopt the Appendix A model rule requiring careful review and certification by signature.
summary: New York Chief Administrative Judge Administrative Order AO/75/2026 adds Part 161, effective June 1, 2026, for all Unified Court System courts in civil and criminal cases. It says attorney and party use of AI to prepare papers should not be prohibited and should not require disclosure upon submission, while offering a model rule for courts that choose one.
text_excerpt: "attorneys and parties should not be required, upon submitting papers, to disclose to the court that they have used AI"
title: Administrative Order AO/75/2026: Part 161, Use of Artificial Intelligence Technology

court: New York Supreme Court, New York County, Civil Term
key_provisions: Motion, hearing, trial, and permitted letter submissions must include a GenAI certification.
If GenAI was used, generated text, citations, quotations, and legal analysis must be reviewed and approved.
The program, documents, and portions drafted by GenAI must be identified.
Use of any AI program during a remote oral argument, conference, or appearance is strictly prohibited.
summary: Justice Nancy M. Bannon’s Part 61 rules, last updated April 2026, require certifications for all motion, hearing, trial, and permitted letter submissions stating whether generative AI was used. If used, the certification must identify the program, documents, and portions drafted, and remote appearances may not use any AI program.
text_excerpt: "Any generative artificial intelligence program must be identified and the documents which include matter generated by the program must be specified"
title: Part 61 Rules: Generative Artificial Intelligence Certification and Remote-Appearance Ban

court: New York Supreme Court, New York County, Matrimonial Division
key_provisions: Applies to Part 44 matrimonial motion submissions.
The rule is adopted pursuant to Part 161 and requires a certification in every motion submission.
If GenAI was used, generated text and legal content must be reviewed for accuracy and approved.
The certification must identify the program, documents, and parts drafted by GenAI.
summary: Justice Ronald Castorina Jr.’s Part 44 rules, effective July 1, 2026, adopt a discretionary Part 161 motion-submission certification. Every motion submission must state whether generative AI drafted listed documents; if so, all generated text, citations, quotations, and legal analysis must be reviewed for accuracy and approved, with program and portions identified.
text_excerpt: "the certification must identify the program, specify the documents that include matter generated by the program"
title: Part 44 Matrimonial Division Rules: Artificial Intelligence Programs

court: New York Supreme Court, New York County, Civil Term
key_provisions: Applies to all motion submissions in Part 34.
The certification must state whether GenAI was used to draft affidavits, affirmations, or memoranda.
If GenAI was used, generated text, citations, quotations, and legal analysis must be reviewed for accuracy and approved.
The program, documents, and drafted parts must be specified.
summary: Justice Dakota D. Ramseur’s Part 34 practices and procedures, revised June 30, 2026, require all motion submissions to include a certification stating whether generative AI was used in drafting affidavits, affirmations, or memoranda of law and, if used, identifying the program, documents, and parts drafted after attorney or self-represented-party review.
text_excerpt: "All submissions with respect to a motion must include a certification by an attorney (or self-represented party)"
title: Part 34 Practices and Procedures: Artificial Intelligence Programs

court: New York Supreme Court, New York County, Civil Term
key_provisions: Applies to all submissions with respect to a motion.
The certification must say whether GenAI drafted covered affidavits, affirmations, or memoranda.
If GenAI was used, generated text, citations, quotations, and legal analysis must be reviewed for accuracy and approved.
The program, documents, and parts drafted by the program must be identified.
summary: Justice Lyle E. Frank’s Part 11 civil rules require every motion submission to include a certification stating whether generative AI drafted any affidavit, affirmation, or memorandum of law. If used, generated text, citations, quotations, and legal analysis must be reviewed for accuracy and approved, and the program, affected documents, and drafted parts must be identified.
text_excerpt: "All submissions with respect to a motion must include a certification by an attorney (or self-represented party)"
title: Part 11 Rules: Use of Artificial Intelligence Programs

court: New York Supreme Court, New York County, Civil Term
key_provisions: Applies to any party using a generative AI tool to prepare filed documents.
The party must disclose AI use and the specific AI tool used.
The party must identify the portion of the filing drafted by AI.
The filing must include a certification of diligent human review for accuracy and applicability.
summary: Justice Kathy J. King’s Part 6 civil term rules require any party using a generative AI tool in preparing documents filed with the court to disclose AI use, disclose the specific tool, identify the portion drafted by AI, and include a certification that the AI work product was diligently reviewed by a human for accuracy and applicability.
text_excerpt: "disclose the specific AI tool used; (3) identify the portion of the filing drafted by AI"
title: Part 6 Rules: The Use of Artificial Intelligence

court: New York Supreme Court, New York County
key_provisions: Applies to all submissions with respect to a motion.
The certification must state whether GenAI was used in drafting covered motion documents.
If GenAI was used, generated text, citations, quotations, and legal analysis must be reviewed and approved.
The program, documents, and parts drafted by GenAI must be specified.
summary: Justice Kathleen Waterman-Marshall’s IAS Part 31 rules require all motion submissions to include a certification stating whether generative AI was used to draft affidavits, affirmations, or memoranda. If used, generated text, citations, quotations, and legal analysis must be reviewed and approved, and the program, documents, and drafted parts identified.
text_excerpt: "the program must be identified and the documents which include matter generated by the program must be specified"
title: IAS Part 31 Rules: Use of Artificial Intelligence in Filings

court: New York Supreme Court, Queens County, Civil Term
key_provisions: Applies to parties appearing pro se or through counsel before Justice Lancman.
Use of GenAI in preparation of filed documents must be disclosed in the document.
The specific AI tool must be identified.
The filer must certify checking AI-drafted content for citations, legal authority, and facts.
sanctions_language: "may result in the denial of any application and the imposition of sanctions."
summary: Justice Mojgan C. Lancman’s Part 20 rules require any party, pro se or represented, using generative AI in preparing documents filed with the court to disclose in the document that AI was used and identify the specific tool. The filer must certify checking AI-drafted content for accuracy, legal authority, citations, and facts.
text_excerpt: "must disclose in the document that AI was used and the specific AI tool that was used"
title: Part 20 Rules: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence

court: New York Supreme Court, New York County, Civil Term
key_provisions: Recording or photographing any court proceeding is strictly prohibited.
The recording prohibition expressly includes AI assistants, bots, and smart glasses.
Court users are reminded of ethical duties requiring accuracy and authenticity in submissions.
summary: Justice Ashlee Crawford’s individual part rules, effective April 8, 2026, prohibit recording or photographing court proceedings, including through artificial intelligence assistants, bots, or smart glasses. The rules also acknowledge AI use in litigation and remind court users of ethical duties requiring accuracy and authenticity in submissions.
text_excerpt: "including through the use of artificial intelligence (AI) assistants or bots, or “smart glasses.”"
title: Individual Part Rules: Artificial Intelligence

court: New York Integrated Domestic Violence Court, New York County
key_provisions: Applies when AI is used to prepare a filing involving substantive legal research and writing.
Counsel or a pro se litigant must add an affirmation at the end of the document.
The affirmation should say the legal research and writing was reviewed and verified for accuracy.
summary: Judge Tandra L. Dawson’s Integrated Domestic Violence Court rules, updated December 3, 2024, require counsel or a pro se litigant to submit an affirmation at the end of any filing involving substantive legal research and writing if AI such as ChatGPT was used to prepare it, and to affirm review and verification for accuracy.
text_excerpt: "counsel or a pro se litigant shall submit an affirmation at the end of the document stating that AI"
title: Integrated Domestic Violence Court Rules: Use of Artificial Intelligence

court: Saratoga County Surrogate’s Court / County Court
key_provisions: The rule governs AI use in preparation and submission of materials to the court.
AI-assisted technology used in evidence creation or editing must be disclosed at submission.
The written certification must identify the type of AI, software or program, role, and final review and approval.
A party may request a Frye hearing for AI-assisted or generated evidence.
sanctions_language: "may face sanctions including, inter alia, striking the document from the record"
summary: Judge Jonathan G. Schopf’s Saratoga County Surrogate’s Court and County Court local rules, effective January 1, 2025, require attorneys, witnesses, or parties to disclose AI-assisted technology used in creating or editing evidence. The written certification must identify the AI type, software or program, role, and final review and approval.
text_excerpt: "must disclose the use of A.I.-assisted technology ... in the creation or editing of any document or material submitted as evidence"
title: Local Court Rules: Use of Artificial Intelligence

court: New York State Supreme Court, Westchester County
key_provisions: Counsel must disclose when a portion of a written submission was generated by AI.
Self-represented parties are subject to the same disclosure requirement.
The disclosure must state what portion of the submission used AI technology.
summary: Justice Helen M. Blackwood’s part rules, amended December 13, 2023, require counsel and self-represented parties to disclose to the court if any portion of a written submission was generated by any form of artificial intelligence and, if so, to identify what portion used that technology.
text_excerpt: "must disclose to the court if any portion of their written submission to the Court was generated"
title: Part Rules: Artificial Intelligence

court: New York State Supreme Court, Westchester County
key_provisions: Counsel must disclose AI-generated portions of written submissions.
Self-represented parties must make the same disclosure.
The disclosure must identify what portion of the submission used AI technology.
summary: Justice David S. Zuckerman’s part rules require counsel and self-represented parties to disclose to the court whether any portion of a written submission was generated by any form of artificial intelligence and, if so, identify the portion that used that technology.
text_excerpt: "must disclose to the court if any portion of their written submission to the Court was generated by any form of artificial intelligence"
title: Part Rules: Artificial Intelligence

court: New York State Supreme Court, Niagara County
key_provisions: Attorneys and parties using AI to prepare papers must understand tool capabilities and limitations.
They must carefully review papers and independently ensure no fabricated or fictitious cases, statutes, or other material.
By signing, the attorney or party certifies that review and absence of fictitious content.
Recording or transcribing phone or Teams proceedings by AI software or tools is not permitted.
sanctions_language: "may be subject to sanction or other remedial action."
summary: Justice Michael J. Norris’s Part 3 rules, as of June 5, 2026, use the Part 161 model-rule language requiring attorney or party users of AI tools in court papers to carefully review and independently ensure no fabricated or fictitious content. The rules also bar recording or transcribing phone or Teams proceedings using AI software or tools.
text_excerpt: "is required to carefully review the paper and independently ensure that it contains no fabricated or fictitious cases"
title: Part 3 Rules: Artificial Intelligence

court: New York Supreme Court, Kings County, Civil Term
key_provisions: Every motion submission must include a GenAI-use certification.
If GenAI was used, generated text, citations, quotations, and legal analysis must be reviewed for accuracy and approved.
The program, documents, and parts drafted by GenAI must be specified.
An attorney discovering hallucinations in an opponent’s submission must immediately inform the court.
summary: Justice Aaron D. Maslow’s Kings County Part 2 rules require every motion submission to certify whether generative AI was used in drafting affidavits, affirmations, or memoranda of law. If used, the certification must identify the program, documents, and drafted parts after review of generated text, citations, quotations, and legal analysis.
text_excerpt: "All submissions with respect to a motion must include a certification either that no generative artificial intelligence program was used"
title: Part 2 Rules: Artificial Intelligence Programs

court: New York Supreme Court, Erie County
key_provisions: The 2025 IAS rules stated that generative AI use was not prohibited.
Counsel or parties using AI resources or material had to identify the AI program.
They had to identify the portion of the filing drafted by AI.
They had to certify human review for accuracy and applicability.

summary: Justice Peter Allen Weinmann’s January 1, 2025 IAS rules stated that generative AI use was not prohibited, but counsel or parties using AI resources or material such as ChatGPT had to disclose or certify the AI program, identify the filing portion drafted by AI, and certify human review for accuracy and applicability.

court: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania
key_provisions: Applies to counsel and self-represented parties in cases assigned to Judge Pratter.
Generative AI use in preparing filings or court correspondence must be disclosed.
The disclosure must be a clear and plain factual statement.
The filer must certify every citation to law or the record as authentic and accurate.
summary: Judge Gene E. K. Pratter’s May 3, 2024 standing order requires counsel or self-represented parties to disclose any generative AI use in preparing a complaint, answer, motion, brief, other paper, or court correspondence. If used, the filer must certify every citation to law or the record as authentic and accurate.
text_excerpt: "disclose that generative AI has been used in any way in the preparation of the filing or correspondence"
title: Standing Order Regarding Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Cases Assigned to Judge Pratter

court: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania
key_provisions: Applies to counsel and pro se litigants using GAI in filings.
Also covers discovery requests, responses, and objections served or delivered.
The procedure requires compliance with Rules 11(b), 26(g), other relevant rules, and ethical rules.
summary: Judge Kelley B. Hodge’s civil procedures state that anyone, counsel or pro se litigant, using generative artificial intelligence in connection with filing a pleading, motion, or paper, or serving or delivering discovery requests, responses, or objections, must comply with Rules 11(b), 26(g), other relevant rules, and applicable ethical rules.
text_excerpt: "using Generative Artificial Intelligence (“GAI”) in connection with the filing of a pleading, motion, or paper"
title: Civil Procedures: Artificial Intelligence

court: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania
key_provisions: Applies to AI use in citations of legal authority filed in cases assigned to Judge Scott.
The filer must disclose that generative AI assisted with citation of legal authority.
The filer must disclose the specific generative AI program used.
The filer must certify every citation of legal authority has been verified as accurate.
summary: Judge Kai N. Scott’s March 3, 2025 standing order requires an attorney or pro se party using generative AI, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, or similar machine-learning tools, in a citation of legal authority filed with the court to disclose AI use, disclose the specific program, and certify every citation is accurate.
text_excerpt: "disclose what specific generative AI program was used, and CERTIFY that each and every citation"
title: Standing Order Re: Artificial Intelligence in Cases Assigned to Judge Scott

court: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania
key_provisions: Applies to attorneys and pro se parties using GenAI to prepare filed papers.
The filer must disclose that GenAI was used to prepare the filing.
The filer must identify the generated portions and the specific tool used and how it was used.
The filer must certify every citation to law or the record was verified under Rule 11 obligations.
sanctions_language: "referral to the appropriate state bar, monetary sanctions, or any other sanction"
summary: Magistrate Judge Caroline Goldner Cinquanto’s policies and procedures require any attorney or pro se party using generative AI to prepare a complaint, answer, motion, brief, or other filed paper to disclose AI use, identify generated portions, identify the specific tool and how it was used, and certify citations to law or record.

title: Judge Goldner Cinquanto’s Policies and Procedures: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence

court: U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania
key_provisions: The policies apply to all matters unless varied by order.
False representations, including AI hallucinations, may subject parties and counsel to sanctions.
Parties and counsel are on notice to double-check citations and reliance on AI in filings.
summary: Judge Mark A. Kearney’s February 2026 policies and procedures warn parties and counsel that false representations, including artificial-intelligence hallucinations, may lead to sanctions under professional-conduct and civil or criminal procedure rules. The policies put parties and counsel on notice to double-check citations and reliance on AI in filings.
